Adversarial Networks can produce highly authentic simulations in complex systems and games, raising the possibility of using these simulations to enhance Markov Decision Processes.  Our study investigated this possibility by using GAN-simulated observations to augment MDPs and assess its effectiveness through policy iteration.  However, simply combining GAN simulations with MDP updates leads to poor results due to GAN's tendency to generate unrealistic outputs when its internal distribution diverges from the target distribution.  To address this challenge, we developed a novel method that utilizes policy evaluation to monitor GAN's performance and lock in its best simulations when it's out of sync.  Our experiments with Atari games revealed that augmenting MDPs with these high-quality simulations accelerates MDP learning and leads to identical performance when using perfect simulations.  When using less accurate simulations, MDPs augmented with these simulations exhibit enhanced learning performance.  Furthermore, results show that MDPs augmented with these simulations can achieve better performance after additional training.  The code used in this study has been made openly accessible on GitHub.  Specifically, we found that augmenting MDPs with these simulations accelerates MDP learning in a subset of easily observable games such as Flappy Bird and Space Invaders but not in games with intricate graphics and visuals such as Breakout and Pong.  Our study lays the groundwork for enhancing learning processes in complex systems and games and raises important questions for the field of GAN research.  Ultimately, we suggest that when MDP learning converges, it may be due to the presence of insufficient data for simulations to be updated.  If this is the case, locking in simulations and utilizing them to augment MDPs may be a viable strategy for augmenting existing data and accelerating MDP learning.  The study also highlights potential avenues for enhancing the performance of both GAN and MDP more broadly.  The code used in this study has been made openly accessible on GitHub at the following link https://github.com/oliverhook/gan_mdp_augmentation.git. A crucial step toward this goal is developing automated CT image analysis techniques to aid in diagnosing and monitoring chronic lung diseases. Such techniques are essential for conducting longitudinal studies on patients with chronic lung disease, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The main objective of this study was to establish a reliable and quick method for extracting useful information from CT images to assess a patient's lung volume. The proposed approach, called CT-Lung-Volume (CLV), is a deep learning framework consisting of two main parts: U-Net for segmenting the lungs and calculating their volumes, along with a time-series analysis model using either ARIMA or LSTM to consider multiple CT scan data. Our investigation, focusing on the transport properties of B doped single-layer MoS$_2$ used as gate-dependent graphene FETs, revealed a highly efficient and pure electrical current with a high mobility.  The integration with graphene allowed us to explore the charge transfer mechanisms at the MoS$_2$-graphene interface.  Our data indicate the formation of spillover molecules at the interface, transferring charge locally to graphene and exhibiting characteristics of a type-I barcus effect.  The effects of light hydrocarbon molecules on charge transfer and mobility in MoS$_2$-graphene interfaces have also been observed, showing the molecules adsorb thermally, aligning their dipoles and increasing the conductivity by filling gaps at the interface.  The findings demonstrate the potential of hybrid structures based on MoS$_2$ and graphene to be used in the development of fast, pure and device-scalable transport channels for quantum device applications.  The charge injection capabilities into MoS$_2$ enabled by these hybrid structures may also be beneficial for the development of novel quantum bits such as the metasurface-based phosphorene-based SQUID.  The high mobility observed in MoS$_2$ systems may be applied in the construction of high speed charge modulation routes for quantum devices. Abstract: 
In this research, we evaluate strategies for handling missing data from repeated measures in clinical trials. A substantial proportion of clinical trials involve patients responding to questionnaires at multiple time points. These data often need to be summarised through an average response using a common metric, such as a change score. When data go missing, either completely or partially, researchers face challenges in how to deal with them. The strategies we examine include deleting cases with missing data, inducing incomplete data patterns, and imputing maximum likelihood. In a small study, we compare these strategies in terms of their effect on inferential statistics. Our findings suggest that deleting cases with missing data significantly reduces the sample size, while inducing incomplete data patterns highlights the importance of designing questionnaires carefully. Imputing maximum likelihood, on the other hand, yields identical results to maximum likelihood estimation when data go missing at random. This study was conducted to aid clinicians in deciding which analytical strategy to use in different scenarios.

networks, including how they pick up on patterns in data and generalize their findings, remains a crucial and complex issue in the field of Artificial Intelligence. The 'Gradients are Gold' theory proposes that the primary means by which neural networks achieve optimization is through the use of gradient descent. However, this approach faces challenges when applied to proxy objectives, such as training accuracy, which falls short of test accuracy. Despite this shortcoming, the 'Gradients are Gold' theory helps explain overfitting and the capacity of neural networks to do so. However, our research demonstrates that there are situations in which gradients are insufficient to account for overfitting occurring. The issue primarily arises when data sets are small, with findings indicating that on larger data sets, overfitting typically occurs after forgetting previous learning, a phenomenon facilitated by gradients. Nevertheless, our research also reveals a new dynamic in which neural networks are capable of engaging in 'overlearning,' forgetting the task itself and shifting away from its initial objectives. The 'Gradients are Gold' theory is unable to account for this behavior, which is attributed to an imbalance that often occurs when optimizing the loss function and the gradients it produces. The discovery of overlearning presents new challenges, which, if left unchecked, may lead to an explosion of results on the test data, a phenomenon referred to as 'double overfitting.' Consequently, double overfitting could potentially be mitigated through increased supervision or data augmentation. Our research also suggests that models exhibiting overlearning tend to have issues with stability and reproducibility, factors that could be addressed through data replay to resolve these issues. By preventing double overfitting, we are able to observe a form of forgiveness in neural networks, a phenomenon that remains unexplained by the 'Gradients are Gold' theory. The occurrence of double overfitting also poses significant risks, as it may lead to a failure to generalize, a phenomenon referred to as'second-order overfitting.' To avoid second-order overfitting, it is essential to take a multi-step approach, using tools such as learning rate scheduling, circular data replay, and test data augmentation to prevent overlearning from occurring in the first place. Our research also suggests that models exhibiting second-order overfitting may suffer from issues with stability and reproducibility, factors that could potentially be addressed through increased supervision or data augmentation. By preventing second-order overfitting, we are able to observe a form of rehabilitation in neural networks, a phenomenon that remains unexplained by the 'Gradients are Gold' theory.

Here, we explore the implications of introducing an inert doublet and a singlet scalar in the context of the Standard Model, assuming the presence of a first-order phase transition in both cases. Additionally, introducing a first-order phase transition in these models results in significant stochastic gravitational wave background predictions, making them potentially detectable in future gravitational wave experiments such as LISA. This study highlights the crucial role of cosmological observations in constraining the parameter space of multi-scalar models, particularly the added scalar component. Longitudinal, multiple-sclerosis lesion data sets are difficult to analyze due to their various characteristics and complexities. Effective semi-supervised techniques for such data sets are in high demand. A novel semi-supervised approach, called active learning (AL), dynamically selects unlabeled samples for more precise labeling based on their potential for improvement. Our proposed framework combines active learning and multiple sclerosis lesion analysis. We introduce a new selection strategy that considers both the importance of labels and the distinct features of the data set. Our framework's performance was tested using an established benchmark dataset called ACIAM, and the results show a substantial improvement in segmentation precision. Specifically, using our approach, we achieved segmentation accuracy of 89%, 87%, and 84% for the training, validation, and test sets respectively. Our framework outperformed a baseline approach in multiple sclerosis lesion analysis, achieving a difference of up to 6% in segmentation precision. The framework's effectiveness was further validated through visual inspections of the segmentation quality. These inspections not only affirmed our numerical outcomes but also highlighted a substantial reduction in false positives. Our proposed framework offers a practical method for semi-supervised learning in the context of multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation. It outperforms baseline approaches in terms of segmentation precision and achieves a high level of performance without requiring any intrinsic enhancements to the underlying segmentation model. Our framework's selection strategy plays a crucial role in its effectiveness, and the results confirm that active learning and multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation are highly compatible. Future research will focus on modifying the selection strategy to make the framework even more robust by accounting for limitations in the manual segmentation process. Additionally, cross-domain applications of the framework will be explored through, for example, breast cancer image segmentation. Our open-source code and data sets are publicly available on the GiannaJ GitHub repository. This accessibility allows other researchers to build and evolve upon our findings. Our framework has the potential to be adapted into a standalone application, and we are currently exploring this option to make the framework user-friendly and efficient for medical professionals. Our ultimate goal is to develop an user-friendly interface that enables multiple sclerosis specialists to integrate the framework into their daily workflow. The framework's effectiveness in a multiple sclerosis context makes it an attractive base for cross-domain applications, and we are confident that further research will yield promising outcomes in this area. This study provides an overview of the core elements of pandemic decision-making, highlights the distinct characteristics of this particular challenge as a "high flow" problem within the broader context of decision-making under uncertainty, and suggests an alternative approach known as "decision-making by iteration" as a potential solution.  Decision-making by iteration serves as a standard framework to address the unique challenges posed by high flow situations, emphasizing ongoing learning, the collaborative identification of effective actions with multiple stakeholders, and the flexible adjustment of decisions in response to evolving conditions.  This study identifies specific decision-making strategies and their related mental frameworks that are particularly relevant to pandemic decision-making, noting how (1) structural frames help address uncertainty at the local level, (2) dynamic frames are necessary for learning under uncertainty at the global level, and (3) both types of frames are interconnected during the pandemic decision-making process.  By understanding decision-making strategies and their mental frameworks, decision-makers can create a conducive environment for evolution and learning to occur, ultimately allowing for more effective pandemic control measures to be implemented.  Ultimately, our approach provides a useful framework for evaluating and comparing different decision-making strategies that rely on learning under a wide range of circumstances, rather than a one-time optimal solution. To address this, we propose a novel approach that aims to incentivize fair behavior without explicitly imposing it. Our method is built on the premise that fair interventions should be seamless to incorporate, and therefore, leverages cooperative game theory to design an attractive alternative for self-interested actors. Specifically, we apply Young's social contract theory, which posits that certain game structures lead to mutually beneficial agreements among players. In our context, we suggest providing individuals with a choice: either adhere to our proposed fairness metric, or engage in a simple auction with the prospect of an even more desirable outcome. This incentive, rooted in game theory's bargaining concept, is expected to motivate cooperation without requiring enforced constraints. Our research presents theoretical underpinnings for this approach, illustrated through an examination of its application to the problem of achieving group fairness in facial attractiveness rating tasks. Our results demonstrate that, under specific conditions, actors are likely to identify and agree upon a group-fair outcome, one that closely aligns with existing metrics, namely median fairness. Additionally, we explored the robustness of this approach in scenarios where different individuals have varying perspectives on what constitutes fairness. Through additional analysis, we found that, in certain instances, negotiations between two actors are likely to result in group-fairness outcomes in line with existing metrics. However, under other circumstances, more nuanced interpretations of fairness are possible. Notably, individual perspectives on fairness may diverge significantly from group-fairness outcomes in these scenarios. Our research sets the stage for future investigations into the practical implementation and evaluation of this approach within practical applications. This work is an extension of our earlier publication in IJCAI 2021, where we first proposed the concept of negotiating a group-fairness outcome. An innovative analytical method utilizing the asymmetry of the muon decay rate in the presence of a transverse magnetic field is proposed, enabling the creation of a novel EDM operator within the framework of perturbative QCD.  By achieving a magnetic asymmetry of $A_r$ and a breakdown of $10^{-18}$ in electron spin $g$-factor in a relatively slow and inexpensive project, this study demonstrates the feasibility of the method and the capabilities of the proposed muon experiment in detecting EDMs, with an emphasis on their potential to explore fast baryon decay patterns and the phenomenon of the breakdown of the $\Delta I=1$ rule in the kaon system, as well as their implications for the advancement of physics beyond the Standard Model.  Specifically, the projected experiment is estimated to be able to detect EDMs of $10^{-22}$ to $10^{-21}$ in baryon matter with lifespans ranging from milliseconds to seconds, thereby providing a crucial means of verifying the $\Delta I=1$ rule and the consistency of the Standard Model through the analysis of kaon decays into pions.  An additional benefit of the proposed experiment is its potential for the direct detection of several new particles and interactions that facilitate baryon decay, including majorons, leptoquarks, and a novel vector-like leptonic preon particle, as well as leptoquark-lepton interactions, as suggested by the preon model. However, the corresponding locations of these features - known as reference points - are often overlooked and left unrecorded. To model these interactions mathematically, a probability distribution function (PDF) is employed to describe both entangled particles and the environment.  A initial assumption, akin to Born's assumption, posits that particles are independent from the environment.  Following this, non-local correlations arise from the non-local connections of space-time and are encapsulated in quantum amplitudes.  A crucial non-local retrieval function (NRF) method then determines environmental characteristics in relation to non-local entanglements.  Utilizing the PDF, transport equations for entangled particles can be formulated a la Liouville-Poisson.  Applying this approach to a specific case study yields insights into non-local retrieval of quantum amplitudes in Born machines.  These Stieltjes-Born machines, characterised by non-local Born series, facilitate the calculation of key environmental properties, such as non-local conditional averages and cross-correlations, and can serve as a theoretical foundation for non-equilibrium electro-transport.  Furthermore, the approach can be adapted to time-dependent quantum systems using an operator formulation, allowing for the generalisation of Wigner distribution functions and Weyl symbols for entangled phase-space distributions.  Initial applications have already provided novel insights into non-local retrieval of quantum amplitudes in Born machines, both in solution-phase studies of small molecules and in experimental investigations of transport across nano-open channels.  Future uses of this approach are expected to enable non-local retrieval of entangled phase-space distributions in quantum systems, thus paving the way for practical applications in quantum transport.  Ultimately, the approach can serve as a theoretical bridge between non-local quantum mechanics and non-equilibrium classical transport.  Conversely, the approach can also be used to derive a macroscopic Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution from a microcanonical ensemble of Liouville-Poisson forms.  These ideas have recently been explored in detail, thus facilitating the transition from quantum entanglements to non-local classical transport.  These ideas have also enabled the generalisation of well-known transport coefficients, such as electrical conductivity, into a non-local framework.  Entangled particles that interact with their environment non-locally can thus be characterised by a set of non-local transport coefficients, thus providing a theoretical foundation for non-local electro-transport.  These ideas have also provided a theoretical basis for the recently-observed non-local retrieval of quantum amplitudes in experiments on small molecules using time-resolved coherent imaging

As a result of this process, a cloud of surrounding matter, the stellar tidal disruption disk, forms around the more massive black hole. This disk plays a crucial role in the formation of a gravitational wave merger event which, given the large number of such systems in the universe, could potentially serve as a detectable and specific cosmic signal called a 'tidal disruption wave.' who died within a specific time frame are referred to as mortality files. They are considered to be essential for policy-making in life insurance industries. However, compounding errors in existing mortality files hampers their utility in accurately projecting future deaths and developing actuarial policies. A novel approach, referred to as Multi-Cohort Lifetable Decomposition (MLD), is introduced in this study to construct more reliable non-marketing mortality profiles. These profiles, based on trends rather than numbers, are more accessible to decision-makers and better respond to changes in cohort sizes. Additionally, this research compares the profiles produced by MLD with those generated by a related method, known as Multipopulation Lifetable Decomposition (MLT). While both methods are related to the former, MLT is susceptible to up/down-shifting issues, where it may project increasing or decreasing mortality profiles for certain cohorts. A significant number of public mortality databases are found to be inadequate for informed decision-making as they are based on a fragmented set of mortality profiles. However, by applying MLD and MLT for US mortality data, it is determined that a single set of unified profiles can be achieved using either of the two methods, effective in representing mortality trends for all cohorts. These profiles are found to be in line with those produced by MLT, except for the fact that MLT is susceptible to up/down-shifting issues, resulting in an incorrect representation of mortality trends for certain cohorts. A potential solution to mitigate such errors is to smooth out the up/down-shifting issues, observed in this study, and it is also found that MLD is more effective in representing mortality trends for small cohorts, although it is capable of producing similar results to MLT for population-level trends. Overall, the study shows that a single set of unified mortality profiles can be generated using either MLD or MLT methods, effective in representing trends for a majority of cohorts, and it is recommended to use MLD as it is more effective in projecting reliable actuarial policies. However, further research is required to develop an alternative approach that is capable of producing profiles for populations with limited data coverage, such as tropical countries in South Asia. Additionally, the topic of informed decision-making is found to be complex and is further explored in a separate study. Among various neutrino sources, the process of electron capture on helium-4 stands out due to its exceptionally high rate of occurrence, making it significant for astrophysical studies and identifiable through distinctive energetic X-ray and NR signatures. While X-ray emissions from this process have been directly observed in specific binary star systems, the associated NR signals remain undetected despite enhanced sensitivity in modern dark matter direct detection experiments. In this work, we employ state-of-the-art computational methods to simulate the NC background produced by neutrino processes such as $^8$B solar neutrinos, $^{12}$C solar neutrinos, and $^{8}$B solar neutrinos combined with CC spallation, and EC, CC, and muon-induced NR backgrounds within the context of a 1 kg Ge-mediated 100 days exposure time. We evaluate these backgrounds within the context of XMASS's sensitivity capabilities and provide projected background expectations for future experiments. Additionally, this study introduces an analytical background model capable of accurately representing the ratio of NC signal to background across various experiments, including future XMASS Stage 2 and similar multi-ton-scale dark matter experiments. Comparing analytical and simulated results, we calculate the signal-to-background ratios for multiple experimental frameworks and assess the significance of their NR triggers. In particular, we investigate the potential implications of these background evaluations within the context of axion dark matter searches. While this study focuses on Ge-based detectors, we demonstrate the applicability of our analytical model across a range of multi-ton-scale dark matter experiments and multiple target materials. This includes calculations involving XENON1T-like Xe, XENON1Y, and Hf-based detectors with various analytical frameworks. We find that high-energy NC backgrounds from CC spallation and EC are primarily discriminable solely through nuclear recoil energy distribution, while mid-energy backgrounds from $^{8}$B solar neutrinos can be identified via combinations of both energy and time dependencies. In contrast, low-energy neutrino backgrounds from $^{8}$B solar neutrinos are primarily accentuated in experimental time profiles. In general, detectors using dense materials and large masses are better equipped to mitigate higher-energy NC backgrounds while offering limited improvements for low-energy backgrounds. We have developed an innovative continuous learning framework, dubbed CLF, which incorporates a unique gradient-based approach that mimics the behavior of spiking neural networks.  By adapting a reassignment mechanism for the selection of hidden neurons and incorporating a spike-based gradient computation method, CLF facilitates the backpropagation of gradients through layers.  This approach has shown superior performance when compared to other methods when tested on tasks requiring strong pattern discrimination and robustness, such as the MNIST and N-MNIST tasks.  Furthermore, CLF has been expanded for use in more complex neuromorphic architectures, including SNNs and HNNs, and has demonstrated promising results on the larger ImageNet dataset.  The CLF framework offers a versatile and adaptable solution for backpropagation-based gradient learning in various neural network configurations.  The implementation of CLF is made available through our source code package on the GH repository.  This includes the CLF code, as well as the custom Python wrapper for the Nauta library, which enables efficient computation on GPUs, and includes existing extensions for tasks requiring multiple input streams, such as the N-MNIST object recognition task. In order to speed up machine learning operations, numerous studies have focused on utilizing Field-Programmable Gate Arrays as they offer a unique blend of performance and power efficiency at the data processing level.  Although there are various architectures within this category, there is a lack of high-level tools and resources suitable for machine learning and data mining tasks.  In response, we have developed a high-level, open-source library named ML-FPGA, designed to leverage the capabilities of Field-Programmable Gate Arrays for machine learning and data mining applications through high-level programming.  This library provides users with the flexibility to employ high-level programming languages, such as Python, for task definition, data management, and output processing, while hardware-specific computations can be defined using the high-level C programming language.  By doing so, users can focus on developing data processing algorithms without needing in-depth knowledge of hardware programming while their designs can be seamlessly executed on various FPGA platforms.  In addition to its high-level framework, ML-FPGA also includes a collection of machine learning and data mining primitives, such as clustering, regression, classification, anomaly detection, and association rule generation, all of which are hardware accelerated to demonstrate the library's capabilities.  In our studies, we have observed significant performance improvements when applying machine learning operations on various data sets, resulting in processing times ranging from a few milliseconds to multiple seconds.  In particular, our experiments have involved the V100 GPU, which, despite outperforming our designs, also experienced much higher power consumption, underlining the importance of integrating machine learning applications with hardware to achieve both accelerated processing and substantial power savings.  In line with this, our library's high-level architecture facilitates the development of data processing applications that are both hardware- and software-agnostic, promoting both technical and resource efficiency.  In terms of technical efficiency, our library's performance results are compared to other state-of-the-art designs, which were found to be either equivalent or outperformed by the ML-FPGA accelerated versions, showcasing the library's effectiveness in terms of processing speed.  In terms of resource efficiency, our experiments have revealed substantial energy savings when applying ML-FPGA, which was found to require only a fraction of the energy consumed by other algorithms, amounting to up to 100-fold reduction in energy usage, ultimately promoting environmental sustainability.  In summary, our high-level library, ML-FPGA, has successfully integrated machine learning and data mining applications with FPGA architectures

has become a significant focus in machine learning due to its various real-world applications. The class-incremental learning approach, used when new classes are added one at a time, is particularly relevant in areas like self-driving cars and medical diagnosis. For instance, when a self-driving vehicle learns from data collected on a new route, it can access only the previously learned classes, making it an ideal application of class-incremental learning. The primary challenge in class-incremental learning lies in how to effectively use old knowledge to re-learn the outdated classes, given that they are no longer accessible. Several approaches have been proposed to address this challenge, including the use of old features, memory systems, and regularization techniques. Each of these proposed methods has its own advantages and drawbacks. For example, using old features can lead to increased storage space needed, memory systems may not always work as intended, and regularization techniques are not specifically designed for this learning scenario. A new approach, called class-incremental learning via episodic memory, addresses the challenge of forgetting previous classes by re-learnable episodic memory systems that store and update features of all classes encountered so far. The proposed method can combine the positive aspects of the other proposed methods, making it a promising solution to the challenge of forgetting previous classes. However, a major issue with the method is its requirement of large feature space storage. Therefore, we propose two efficient storage methods to mitigate this challenge: a loss-calculated feature transform (LCFT) that transforms the old features into a compact space using a transform derived from the old loss function of each class, and a feature-domain transformation (FDT) that transforms the old features into a condensed feature space using a non-linear mapping. The two methods can work together to combine the strengths of both, or work independently. The methods were tested on several datasets and the results were compared against other state-of-the-art methods. The results were found to be on par with the state-of-the-art results, making the proposed approach a promising solution to the challenge of forgetting previous classes in class-incremental learning. The methods were implemented in an open-source framework available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenVee/cil_episodic_memory.git. The framework includes all the source codes of the experiments mentioned in this thesis. The framework also includes a new approach to combining the features of the old and new domains, and the features of the primary memory and the episodic memory. The framework was tested on several datasets and the results were found to be promising

  Ensuring quality of service in these networks has become increasingly critical.
  As a result, wireless operators face significant challenges in optimizing network performance, mainly due to the difficulty of accurately predicting traffic patterns and the complexity of implementing quality-of-service models.
  One innovative approach to overcome these challenges involves employing artificial intelligence models, particularly Deep Neural Networks. 
  Although the feasibility of using artificial intelligence models in this context is theoretically supported, a comprehensive investigation of their effectiveness is still pending.
  This study presents a novel method to assess the potential of artificial intelligence models in facilitating quality-of-service modeling in wireless networks.
  By leveraging these models, network administrators can generate practical input for quality-of-service models, which will subsequently simplify the creation of quality-of-service models and enhance network management capabilities.
  The research provides a new framework for quality-of-service modeling and conducts an in-depth performance assessment, supported by real-world case studies.
  The findings suggest that artificial intelligence models can indeed be employed as quality-of-service models under specific network conditions.
  The proposed quality-of-service models based on artificial intelligence are adaptable and applicable in a range of network configurations, including both centralized and decentralized networks.

an online social platform can facilitate crucial insights for an online community's governance and security. Given that visualisation tools facilitate exploration but cannot ultimately replace an in-depth network analysis, and since many social media platforms revoke access to interaction data following account deactivation, our study simulates a representative Facebook network. By creating and analysing a large-scale Facebook network comprising over 18 million users, our central inquiry centers around the centrality measurements of accounts within the simulated network. Through statistical analysis, our findings reveal the prevalence of exceptionally central accounts, the interdependence of various centrality metrics, and the centralisation level in our simulated Facebook network. By comparing our findings with actual Facebook profiles, our study validates the importance of account age as a determining factor for exceptional centrality and highlights the need for more sophisticated metrics to assess centralities on social media. Furthermore, our investigation into in-degree centrality reveals the existence of'social workers' with an abundance of friends, while our focus on various centrality metrics confirms the presence of elite groups within these categories. By identifying key characteristics associated with exceptional centrality, our study lays the groundwork for crucial security implications by revealing the vulnerability of prominent accounts to targeted attacks within the simulated Facebook network. As such, our study suggests that social media platforms requiring prolonged user engagement could potentially safeguard against malicious account takeover. Ultimately, by performing a comprehensive analysis of a large-scale Facebook network, our study contributes to the body of knowledge on social media architecture and its associated security implications. As a visualisation tool-based exploration is insufficient for an in-depth analysis of online social platforms, our study prioritizes an in-depth investigation into the network architecture of a large-scale Facebook network comprising over 18 million users. As such, our study contributes significantly to the existing literature on social media architecture and its associated security implications. Although our study prioritizing a centrality-based analysis may appear as an alternative to existing work focusing on additional aspects of Facebook architecture, our research indicates a pressing need for further investigations into the network architecture as a whole. As an initial step in this direction, our study simulates a large-scale Facebook network comprising over 18 million users to explore an additional aspect of the network architecture. As such, our study highlights the presence of'social workers' within prominent accounts with an abundance of friends in in-degree centrality, while our focus on various centrality metrics confirms the presence of elite groups within these categories. As an initial exploration into this additional aspect of the network architecture, our study contributes significantly to the existing literature on social media architecture and its associated security

Traditional MARL methods frequently rely on local reactions to their surroundings, neglecting implicit communication channels. Focusing solely on local reactions may hinder implicit communication-based reward access and reduce the learning efficiency.   A fundamental policy evaluation method compares how well a revised policy performs in comparison to the status quo, with the policy being considered effective if it yields better outcomes.
  However, in scenarios where an organization's goal is to prevent a certain event, such as cases being tried in court, an opposite approach is employed.
  Specifically, an adverse policy is defined as one that minimizes the likelihood of a specific adverse event occurring, as opposed to a mitigating policy, which is designed to control the occurrence of the same adverse event but may also result in additional negative consequences.
  Both types of policies are evaluated through a specific decision-making process known as an experiment.
  A well-known framework, APT, is used to accurately calculate both the advantage and potential drawback of an adverse policy in comparison to the status quo.
  A specific application of the APT framework is the risk assessment method, where an adverse policy is evaluated based on its ability to reduce a specific risk while minimizing any potential negative consequences.
  In order to accurately evaluate an adverse policy in scenarios where cases are moved to different courts, a modified risk assessment method is proposed.
  In addition to proposing this new method, a public policy evaluation tool, called the APT Calculator, is also introduced and can be accessed through its associated website. 
  This tool allows for the easy computation of an adverse policy's evaluation based on any given case distribution, as well as its corresponding potential drawback. 
  In the context of the Risk Assessment Method, specific values need to be known in order to accurately evaluate an adverse policy's ability to reduce a specific risk while minimizing any potential negative consequences.
  In an effort to provide support for this method, a risk assessment calculator is also introduced and can be easily accessed through its associated website. 
  In this paper, both the APT Calculator and the Risk Assessment Calculator will be presented in depth and their functionality will be demonstrated. 
  In addition to this, the potential drawback of an adverse policy is also defined as the difference between the amount of benefit an adverse policy is capable of providing and the amount of benefit a mitigating policy is also capable of providing.
  In order to accurately evaluate an adverse policy's potential drawback, a specific amount of a specific variable is required in order to accurately compare both types of policies.
  In an effort to provide some data for this variable, a public database, called the Adverse Policy Oracular Source of information, is also proposed and provides users with access to a collection of adverse policy evaluations.

We explore specific examples from experiments and simulations of disordered systems in equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium settings. We discuss how statistical properties of information mutual entropy are connected to the idea of an 'information gap' in systems that involve an information source and an information receiver. Compressed information is related to the concept of an 'channel', with a focus on its maximum capacity that does not depend on the specifics of the data transmitted. We analyze these concepts through experiments based on a binary system, including a simple physical model that involves magnetic particles in a trapped ion configuration and a more complex study of a system of metamagnetic loops that adapt to changes using an elastic mechanism. We compare the findings from these experiments with a simulation of an information exchange system that involves a sender, a channel, and a receiver in a system of connected loops that adapt to changes, with the possibility of adjusting the channel to maximize compressed information transfer. We examine the statistical properties of information mutual entropy in a system of connected loops that adapt to changes and a system of disconnected loops that interact thermally, using a model that represents multiple loops attached to a fixed ion that interacts with a heating mechanism. We investigate the compressed information in these systems by analyzing the process of data compression through an adaptive encoding scheme that adjusts an effective temperature based on probability distribution characteristics. We compare the compressed information in these systems to the compressed information in a system of connected loops that adapt to changes and a system of disconnected loops that interact thermally, using a model that represents multiple loops attached to a fixed ion that interacts with a heating mechanism. While some loss functions have set new benchmarks, they often require significant modifications to the training code, which is a major drawback. Our research introduces an orthogonal approach by creating a loss pooling layer that supports multiple loss functions in a unified way, eliminating the need for code changes. What's more, this layer can be trained without modifications to the existing network structure, making it a truly plug-and-play solution. We have evaluated our method with six widely used loss functions and the results show that they outperform the current state-of-the-art in cross-entropy and softmax regressions, while also reducing memory usage and computation time. Furthermore, we have developed a new softmax loss function, called Localized Softmax (LS), which mitigates numerical computation issues and offers a (small) accuracy gain over the traditional softmax function.  It also offers a (small) accuracy gain over the existing Quad softmax function.  It has been tested on cross-validation and the result show that it perform similarly to the current state-of-the-art loss function.  The impact of the number of neurons per group has been studied and the result show that a small group size perform better than a large group size.  Practical implementation of the loss function reveal that it can be implemented using GLU layer with one addition parameter per group. cameras are increasingly used in human
machine interaction research due to their superior 3D recognition capabilities
at high frame rates exceeding 50Hz, which far surpass traditional stereo
cameras by a considerable margin. These cameras, however, are susceptible to
noise stemming from internal light sources, ambient environments, and the
camera's own transmissions. Noise severely hampers 3D data quality, impairing
its usability. Effective noise reduction methods are pivotal for 3D data
quality, enabling its application in human movement analysis, such as
tracking hand gestures. We introduce a real-time 3D restoration approach,
combining a spatiotemporal noise model with a convolutional neural network
framework, specifically tailored for single-photon ToF cameras. Our method,
utilizing sequences of 3D points over time, isolates the camera's acquisition
process from existing noise models. Experimental results demonstrate that our
real-time approach outperforms existing deep learning-based methods by
approximately 2.5dB in restoring 3D hand motion captured at 51.8Hz. Our
research offers a versatile, high-performance restoration tool for a range
of single-photon camera models, promoting its adoption in various real-time
applications, such as human movement analysis in human machine interaction.

Our goal is to develop an effective transfer learning method that minimizes the influence of noisy interactions during training, enabling models to achieve high transfer performance. To this end, we propose an innovative approach that combines model-based and model-free techniques with a probabilistic regularization framework. This approach aims to optimize the uncertainty of state predictions to reduce the impact of noisy interactions. Our method can be widely applied to various deep reinforcement learning algorithms and has the advantage of being adaptable to different scenario requirements. It is capable of switching between different transfer learning modes, such as single-task or multi-task transfer, without any modifications to the existing code. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves the transfer performance of popular deep reinforcement learning agents, including Proximal Policy Optimization and Deep Q-Network, under various conditions. Furthermore, the impact of different design choices on the performance of our approach was evaluated through ablation studies, which highlight the critical role of model-based state prediction in addressing the lack of transferability in model-free agents. These findings serve as a starting point for further research into the therapeutic potential of model-based techniques for addressing transferability challenges in deep reinforcement learning. Until now, there has been a lack of research on the development of agents capable of learning to play Atari games through both model-based planning and intrinsic curiosity-driven reinforcement learning. Our method overcomes the limitations of both approaches by introducing a novel multi-stage training framework that switches between these two training methods. Our approach not only achieves state-of-the-art transfer performance but also achieves it with significantly fewer interactions with the environment, less memory requirements, and a much simpler architecture. Our results show that the combination of model-based planning and intrinsic curiosity-driven reinforcement learning yields a highly efficient transfer learning agent. It is worth noting that the observation space of our test environment, Breakout, is significantly larger than the others in the field. Building on its technological principles, the concept of the photonic spike has been applied to the development of a new theoretical model that describes the collective detection mechanism of the PLL, and this model is consistent with the experimental results that were previously mentioned. We focused on signals lasting up to 100 seconds after the merger, considering various physical processes associated with the post-merger remnant's life. To simplify the analysis, we developed a model based on symmetric eigenfunctions of the Merger-Echo's radial potential. Successful detections were achieved within the studied time frame, with most signals related to the remnant's mass loss through gravitational radiation. As such, this transition can be characterized as a combination of both electronic and phonon-driven mechanisms that share a fundamental connection to the presence of a large orbital degeneracy seen in this class of materials. However, graph structures that reflect transitive relations often cause issues with query efficiency, leading to subpar performance due to the limitations of predicate handling.  Existing indexing methods, although able to improve query speed, typically fail to address the impact of data distribution and may not account for the specific characteristics of a given database.  In contrast, our proposed adaptive index serves as a data-driven guide to determine suitable indexing parameters by taking into consideration the data distribution and the specific properties of a given database, ultimately providing informed configuration options to users. In developing our index, we employ a data-driven approach combining theoretical modeling and experimental validation to ensure accuracy, and our results demonstrate the efficacy of our method, showcasing significant improvements in the quality of the suggested indices compared to traditional methods based on secondary memory or graph indices.  Moreover, this index does not depend on the query workload; our method outperforms the best known method for a specific dataset.  As part of our contribution, we create a publicly accessible repository containing the necessary code, data sets, and experimental results, enabling users to compare our method to other available configurations.  Initially, our method will be made available through a standard software release, before eventually being integrated into database management systems, where it will provide users with informed configuration options to improve query performance. Several successful teams in international programming competitions, like Google's CodeJam and ICPC, have been studied, revealing that their key contributors typically have programming experience of at least five years. These notable teams, consisting of multiple members, have demonstrated better performance in time-sensitive programming challenges, and their productivity is largely unaffected by the number of team members, as long as there is a skilled lead to manage the workload and distribute tasks efficiently. The success of these teams can be attributed to several crucial factors, including their ability to collaborate effectively, receive guidance from experienced members, and take advantage of collective strengths. Ultimately, the optimal team size for a given problem will depend on the specific skills and dynamic of the members, but a two-person team appears to be a good general minimum. As for solo competitors, their performance is more unpredictable and heavily reliant on individual factors, such as their programming ability and time management skills. Despite this, there are instances of highly successful solo competitors, like Adam Yala in the 2020 USACO Pro Competition, and their success can be attributed to their exceptional skills and ability to adapt quickly to the given problems. In contrast to team composition, which is relatively consistent across successful competitors in certain competitions, the solo path to success is more isolated and requires a higher level of individual skill, but it is still achievable. 
  Overall, the key to becoming a great programmer takes time, patience, and dedication, whether one chooses to compete individually or as part of a team. 
  This study is based on an analysis of programming competition data and conversations with top competitors, and it provides insight into the importance of team dynamics in these competitions. 
  The research highlights the significance of lead experience and collaboration in successful team programs, and it notes that a two-person team is an optimal way to leverage these strengths. 
  Additionally, the study explores the varying factors that contribute to individual success in these competitions, and it emphasizes the crucial role of programming ability and problem-solving skills. 
  One of the major challenges in analyzing programming competition data is the lack of publicly available information on individual participants, and researchers must often rely on partial data for their studies. 
  This problem arises from the differing goals and frameworks of individual competitors, and teams have varying incentive structures that affect data availability.

Dense image matching is a fundamental low-level operation in computer vision, where high-density matches provide essential geometric and texture information. Traditionally, dense matching has relied on feature descriptors that are inherently independent of images, but which often struggle to retain or enhance match density across moderate transformations. To overcome this limitation, our work introduces an innovative approach that develops image-dependent dense matching. This approach employs an innovative network, known as the Depth-guided Descent-ascending Matching network, which is driven by a dynamic search range and a dynamic weight adjustment. Our approach provides three key advantages. Firstly, it develops a Depth-guided Descent-ascending Cascade Shift (DADS) filter to refine matches at a pixel level, thereby retaining more matches and achieving greater robustness. Secondly, it introduces a Dynamic Descent-ascending Weight Adjustment (DDWA) module to adjust weights of stochastic experts at a feature element level, thereby retaining more matches and achieving greater robustness. Thirdly, it develops a Dynamic Search Range Module (DSRM) to adjust search ranges of stochastic experts at a feature element level, thereby retaining more matches and achieving greater robustness. Our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of match density across multiple datasets. To evaluate our approach, we designed a benchmark dataset consisting of six image pairs derived from SUN360 and MITY600. Our approach achieved significant improvements in terms of match density, with speeds up three times faster than existing methods. Despite their established effectiveness, the deep learning community has historically been restricted by hardware limitations.  To break down these barriers, automating the process of mapping deep learning algorithms to hardware has become a pressing need.  This need is driven by two primary factors:  Firstly, significant expertise is required to design efficient deep learning accelerators, and secondly, these accelerators are often compromises between multiple objectives, such as speed, size, and energy efficiency.  This study proposes a novel deep learning hardware design automation framework, known as LibShuffle, that addresses these challenges by allowing users to describe their requirements through a simple, structured interface. network classifications involve combining many fewer "witness sets" of classified examples, each set having a small number of examples. Despite the potential of these methods, their practical application has been hindered until now by the lack of publicly accessible, implementable tools to generate the required witness sets for complex classifications. We provide a solution by introducing an efficient algorithm to create well-certified witness sets for classifications that involve high-dimensional inputs and numerous classes by leveraging certain properties of randomized neural networks that produce noisy, categorical outputs. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by achieving the first full formal security verification of the CNN model for classifications of high-dimensional MNIST images, a result that previous research had not been able to attain. The experiment also shows that the number of examples required for such security verification is relatively small, roughly 0.1% of the total number of possible input examples. Further research is also conducted to analyze how different network architectures and hyperparameters affect the number of required examples. We found that randomized neural networks with specific architectures and hyperparameters outperform other certified methods in terms of scalability, although other methods may have stronger formal certifiable bounds. We provide an open-source implementation of this approach in the form of a Python package called "Annotated Neural Networks" and we believe that this package can be used for other research in the field of formal security verification of neural networks. We successfully applied this approach to other classifications of images, specifically K-Means clustering on CIFAR10, achieving a significant reduction in the number of required examples, roughly 100 times. We obtained this result by providing additional context information, specifically the weights of the clustering model. We also conducted a series of experiments to analyze how different training algorithms and protocols can be applied to formally secure neural networks, specifically Randomized Neuron Split Hybrid Training (RNS-HT) which combines randomized neural networks with the neuron split training protocol. We found that the convergence of the security verification can be affected by specific parameters of the algorithm and protocol, namely the number of iterations, the learning rate, and the randomization iterations. We provided bounds on the number of iterations required to achieve convergence of the security verification. We took an additional step in the research by formally securing a specific cryptographic primitive, the block cipher family, the LBlock, by applying the certified machine learning approach, formally securing classifications of binary images, specifically, the binary supermesh database. In order to fully utilize their capabilities, an efficient control mechanism is required.  Logically reprogrammable nonvolatile memory (LRN) technology, however, offers a more efficient alternative to traditional FPGA and SRAM-based memory technologies for neuromorphic systems.  This paper demonstrates how LRN and memristive LRN arrays can be used to develop adaptive weight update and online learning circuits for spiking neuromorphic circuits, by leveraging the ability to store multiple sets of weights and gate access levels with multiplexers.  This design results in significant weight update and learning energy savings of multiple orders of magnitude, when compared to traditional LRN-based update circuits.  This advantage is especially apparent when using memristive LRN arrays for weight update, yielding an additional ~2 orders of magnitude in energy savings over traditional LRN arrays.  This substantial improvement in energy efficiency enables memristive LRN arrays to almost match the energy efficiency of CMOS transistors, making them a more competitive option for neuromorphic systems.  This work also proposes a novel learning scheme that can take advantage of the LRN's reprogrammability and multiplexed access, while maintaining convergence in a single-pass online learning scenario.  This scheme has the advantage of reduced memory requirements, lower computational overhead, and superior sample efficiency, when compared to traditional online learning schemes.  Finally, the proposed LRN-based weight update and learning circuits were verified with both LRN and memristive LRN arrays, modeling spike trigger updates and memristive threshold crossings, respectively.  Design examples were demonstrated on 28nm technology, resulting in a substantial reduction in static and dynamic energy per operation for the LRN-based weight update and learning circuits, when compared to traditional LRN-based update circuits.  These experiments also verified the feasibility of the proposed LRN-based weight update and learning circuits, when paired with memristive devices, due to their comparable or superior performance to CMOS technology.  Overall, the proposed LRN-based weight update and learning circuits offer a promising path towards highly efficient neuromorphic circuits, when combined with memristive devices. Despite existing theories related to optimization and inductive biases, there is a lacking comprehension regarding generalization. We propose the Fundamental Generalization Theorem, which asserts generalization arises from a combination of fundamental inductive biases and a generalization limit, not dependent on optimization processes. The generalization limit is inherently present within any reasonable network architecture. Although the generalization theorem does not require an optimized optimizer, we found that Tikhonov regularization within gradient descent can enhance generalization, achieving consistency with the generalization theorem's predictions up to a certain margin. We verified these findings through the application of the Binary Linear Model as a benchmark case. Moreover, under the assumption that the Binary Linear Model holds for all data points, we developed an approach to estimate the generalization threshold based on data accessibility. With the generalization theorem in mind, we analyzed several neural network architectures, revealing that generalization performance may severely decline when dimensions exceed a certain threshold, a phenomenon consistent with observed numerical results. Thus, it is evident that a substantial depth and width in neural networks do not necessarily ensure superior generalization performance. The findings provided sufficient evidence for the generalization theorem's validity and shed light on the understanding of generalization in neural networks. The generalization theorem's implications also offer a possible explanation for the success of overparameterized neural networks, which is an area of ongoing research. The theoretical framework proposed may also be extended to other machine learning models. We discover that the disparity in the number of connections for elements in these networks is a geodesic (the shortest path) property and that it significantly impacts the shift in their characteristics over time. We observe that networks with a specific connection pattern that is well-suited to their geometry (the elements are arranged in a two-dimensional plane and each neighbor is connected to one another) experience a relatively slow shift in their characteristics over time. A novel deep learning-based approach is introduced to automatically identify and segment the abnormal airways in CT scans, thereby facilitating the early diagnosis of this condition. The approach consists of two pre-trained U-Net models, one optimized for left lung and the other for right lung lesions, to enhance its versatility. A two-step training mechanism is employed to refine the models' performance by first segmenting the lungs and then identifying the abnormal airways within the already-Partitioned lung segments. Evaluation results of the approach on a large dataset of 1200 CT scans indicate high accuracy with an Dice coefficient as high as 0.90 and accurate presence estimation with an IoU score of 0.95. Furthermore, the approach demonstrates excellent clinical applicability by requiring only a few user interactions to achieve such high performance. Additionally, the approach's fine-tuning capability allows for unsupervised segmentation of new patients by adapting the model with only a few labeled airway segments from a single new patient. This in turn promotes its practical use in medical practice. As a secondary contribution, a novel metric for evaluating segmentation performance is proposed based on the presence of adjacent structures, which can aid in identifying the irregular inner airway wall for more accurate diagnosis. The proposed approach outperforms significantly a baseline U-Net model on a large dataset of 1200 CT scans with a high Dice coefficient of 0.85 and accurate presence estimation with an IoU score of 0.90. Moreover, the approach's performance exhibits significant improvement over a baseline method on a subset of 300 CT scans with an increased Dice coefficient of 0.10 and accurate presence estimation with an increased IoU score of 0.10. Evaluation results of the approach on a subset of 600 CT scans indicate high reliability with an increased Dice coefficient of 0.05 and accurate presence estimation with an increased IoU score of 0.05. Furthermore, the approach's performance is comparable to that of a human radiologist on a subset of 100 CT scans with a mean Dice coefficient of 0.87 and a mean IoU score of 0.85. These results indicate the potential of the approach in automatically identifying the abnormal airways in a chest X-ray, thereby facilitating early diagnosis of pulmonary arterial hypertension. Current methods for synthesizing environmental maps often fail because they rely on weak correlations between real lighting conditions and map intensities. Existing high-quality datasets for EMaps also have this issue, making them unsuitable for training models that predict lighting conditions accurately. Our solution to this problem is to develop a new dataset called ArtMaps, which features auto-generated artificial EMaps that can be easily differentiated from the real ones. By establishing a clear relationship between lighting conditions and map intensities in this dataset, our novel approach for EMaps synthesis becomes feasible, and it consistently outperforms other methods in translating lighting conditions to EMaps. Although our method is based on neural networks, it doesn't require any further training compared to other methods in the same field. Our ArtMaps dataset is available at https://github.com/edgarborja/artmaps.
